2.text: instance, in a tale about Eleˊndi and his sons, a little boy, the grandson

3.text: of the hero, plays all the time at shooting with a bow, not even taking time

4.text: to sleep. One day his father says jestingly, “Here is a blade of grass. Try

5.text: and hit its stem.” He made for the boy a small arrow of a piece of kettle

6.text: iron. The boy shot and cut the blade in two. In the morning they continued

7.text: their journey and met a Taˊn˙ñɪn. “Oh!” says the father, “you are but a

8.text: child.” — “What of it?” says the boy. “And what will your mother say?

9.text: Well, let us go near. Then you sit down at a safe distance. I will fight

10.text: against that man with my lance. However, I may get tired. Then I shall

11.text: return, and you shall string your little bow. I shall look at you, thus, and

12.text: cross the road near to you. Then you shall shoot at his forehead. Try at

13.text: least to cut the skin on his forehead.” The father began the fight with the

14.text: Taˊn˙ñɪn, became tired, and retreated towards the place were his child was

15.text: sitting. Then the boy strung his bow and shot and cut the skin on the fore-

16.text: head of the Tan˙ñɪn. “Oh! this is how you take away our herds. You are

17.text: strong through the aid of a boy. We do not act thus. Your strength lies in

18.text: your union with boys.” — “Ah!” says the father, “I have created a strong

19.text: man for times to come, one who will take the property of all those living

20.text: in the country around us. I must be very good indeed.”

21.text: After several years, in a quarrel with his father about the distribution of

22.text: tobacco, the son says, “If I had not then cut that broad forehead, we could

23.text: not have smoked at this time.”¹

24.text: As in other hero-tales of the Chukchee, the details are given in a manner

25.text: that is very true to life. Other instances of the same kind might be added.

26.text: The life of children among the Maritime Chukchee is less pleasant.

27.text: Maritime villages are filthy in comparison with the ever-changing camp of the

28.text: Reindeer people. The interior of the house, where the children spend a

29.text: considerable part of their time, is black from smoke, and full of heavy odors.

30.text: Food, too, is less abundant, and the supply less certain. On the other hand,

31.text: the years of leisure and play are much longer here than among the reindeer-

32.text: breeders. The reindeer-breeding Chukchee send boys of ten, and girls hardly

33.text: older than that, to help in tending the herd. I remember having met one

34.text: summer-time two such young reindeer-breeders, a boy and a girl. They were

35.text: from ten to twelve years old. They were walking through the bushes quite

36.text: alone, staff in hand, and wallet on back. They had to walk some ten miles

37.text: before they could reach their herd. It was strange to see these young children

38.text: wandering in the bush without any protection and shelter. While with the

39.text: herd, the children have their share of all the troubles and care of guarding

40.text: the restive animals. Of course they sleep more than the adult herdsmen, and

41.text: do not run about so much; still their life is hard enough. When three or
